Game: This is not a game to win: the same gray ring crosses two squares, and sliding one square can make its two halves look different.
How to play: Move the six sliders to change the square shades, the ring shade and the slide. Drag the slide dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys, then press Reset to start over.

Look for the math

The original page calls this Koffka's example of simultaneous contrast: the same gray can look different when its neighbours change. The live article no longer embeds the Java applet, so the drawing here follows the archived applet itself, captured on 9 May 2008. Everything below is geometry and shading; there is no score to win.

What the applet draws

Two equal squares sit side by side in a canvas width × height. The applet takes side = round(min(width/2, height)) − 40, puts the squares at the middle of the canvas, and centres a circle on the line between them. Its outer radius is round((side/2)·Max/100·7/8); the inner disk split into two halves has radius round(r·9/10·Min/100). The ring is therefore a narrow band: the inner disk never reaches past it. See geometry for the idea of fixing a shape by a few numbers.

One uniform gray

SetGrayColor() builds all three shades with Color(t, t, t), where t = slider/100. The whole outer circle is filled with that one gray, and only the smaller inner disk is repainted, left half in the left square's shade and right half in the right square's shade. The page's claim of “an uniform gray shade” is confirmed: the band between the two radii is a single shade on both sides. The test checks every one of the 101³ tone triples against java.awt.Color's float conversion, and samples pixels from a second transcription of Draw() at every Min and Max with several slides. What the eye makes of that shade belongs to a contrast effect, not to the arithmetic.

Sliding the two halves

The H scrollbar runs from −50 to 50. Draw() moves the right square, with its half of the ring, vertically by dy = round(side·H/100) and repaints the strips it leaves behind; the left half does not move. At H = 0 the two halves meet in one circle. The page says the halves “acquire independent identities” when slid: the test confirms the physical change — one half shifts by dy, the other stays, and both keep the same gray — while the different appearance is the perceptual claim the page is illustrating. The slide dot on this page is a modern convenience for moving H; it adds no new rule.

Ranges, rounding and shades

Each AWT scrollbar was built as Scrollbar(0, value, 5, minimum, maximum). Because the visible thumb is 5 units wide, the reachable maxima are 100 rather than the declared 105 (and 50 rather than 55 for H). The core keeps those reachable ranges and the applet's starting values. Java's integer divisions truncate toward zero, Math.round rounds halves up, and Color(float) converts each component with floor(t·255 + 0.5), so 50 becomes 128 and 100 becomes 255. The test compares the core with a literal second transcription over all 101 × 61 × 101 geometry settings at three canvas sizes. The page's sentence that spatial configuration “may significantly influence contrast perception” is qualitative; there is no number on the page to prove or refute.

Try left shade 0, right shade 100 and ring gray 50, then slide H all the way up and down: both halves of the ring are still gray 128.
